name: Vbeam Perfecta
lead: Vbeam Perfecta is a pulsed dye laser (PDL) system made by Candela that emits yellow light at 595 nm, a wavelength absorbed by hemoglobin. It is used in dermatology for vascular lesions such as port-wine stains, hemangiomas, facial telangiectasias and rosacea-related redness, and some practices offer it for scars and general facial redness [1].

Pulsed dye lasers have long been treated in the medical literature as the standard approach for port-wine stains [2][3]. Evidence for purely cosmetic uses, such as photoaging, is limited to small studies [4].
infobox: Variable pulse duration; cryogen Dynamic Cooling Device [1]

paras: According to an AI-generated encyclopedia entry, Candela introduced its first pulsed dye laser in the 1980s, developed from selective photothermolysis work done with Massachusetts General Hospital, and the Vbeam line followed in the early 2000s, with the Perfecta model launched in 2005 [1]. That account is not independently confirmed in the other sources reviewed.
The same source describes a 595 nm wavelength, adjustable pulse durations of roughly 0.45 to 40 ms, spot sizes of about 3 to 12 mm and a cryogen spray cooling device that protects the epidermis [1].

In selective photothermolysis the laser light is absorbed by oxyhemoglobin, heating and closing targeted vessels while sparing surrounding tissue [1]. Variable pulse settings, including stacking multiple lower-fluence pulses, have been studied as a way to heat vessels while reducing purpura (bruising) [5].

Most published work concerns medical vascular indications rather than appearance enhancement in healthy skin. A randomized comparison of treatment with the pulsed dye laser versus wait-and-see for superficial infantile hemangioma has been published [2]. Port-wine stains are described in the literature as a condition where PDL is considered the gold standard, although a large share of lesions may be refractory, prompting trials of add-ons such as topical rapamycin [3].

A randomized trial of a 595-nm laser examined fresh surgical scars [6], and a blinded randomized trial using a 595-nm laser to create bruises tested whether topical arnica hastened bruise resolution [7]. A pulse-stacking study examined whether stacked low-fluence pulses affect outcomes in vascular lesions [5].
Registered trials include a 20-person study of the Vbeam Prima for photoaged facial skin [4] and a 34-person study combining PDL with oxymetazoline cream for erythematotelangiectatic rosacea [8].

Bruising (purpura) is a recognized effect of pulsed dye laser treatment, and several studies and cooling features aim to reduce it [5][7]. Descriptions of the device note that cryogen cooling is intended to lessen discomfort and protect the epidermis [1].

timeline.event: Candela's early pulsed dye laser reportedly receives FDA clearance for vascular lesions (per Grokipedia). [1]

card.summary: Candela's 595 nm pulsed dye laser, a clinic mainstay for redness and vascular lesions; cosmetic-only evidence is thin.
card.note: Evidence is strongest for medical vascular lesions; bruising is a common effect.

quick.overview:
Vbeam Perfecta is a pulsed dye laser from Candela used by dermatologists for port-wine stains, hemangiomas, broken capillaries and persistent facial redness.

Its research base is mainly medical vascular conditions. Studies of it for general appearance, such as photoaging, are small.
quick.mechanism: 595 nm light is absorbed by hemoglobin, heating and closing small vessels. A cryogen spray cools the skin surface during each pulse.
quick.risks: Bruising (purpura) and temporary redness or swelling are recognized effects; settings such as pulse stacking have been studied to reduce purpura.
